title: Inventory Management & Lean Manufacturing
description: Just-in-time, material requirements planning, the seven wastes of lean, and how reducing waste improves production.
content_html:
Managing What You Need, When You Need It

Every manufacturing business must manage its inventory — the raw materials, components and finished goods it holds in stock. Too much stock ties up capital, occupies warehouse space, risks obsolescence, and can mask inefficiencies in the production process. Too little stock means production lines stop because a critical component has run out. Inventory management is the discipline of finding and maintaining the right balance, using systems such as just-in-time (JIT) and material requirements planning (MRP) to coordinate supply with demand.

Just-in-Time (JIT) Manufacturing

Just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing is an approach in which materials arrive exactly when they are needed in the production sequence — not before and not after. Originated and perfected by Toyota in Japan, JIT aims to eliminate the waste of holding inventory. Advantages include: reduced warehousing costs, lower capital tied up in stock, reduced risk of materials becoming obsolete or damaged in storage, and the ability to respond quickly to changes in customer demand. Disadvantages include: very high dependency on supplier reliability — if a delivery is late, the production line stops; there is no buffer stock to absorb disruptions; and the approach requires excellent supplier relationships, accurate demand forecasting and a very disciplined production schedule. JIT works best in stable, predictable production environments.

Key Fact

Just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing orders and delivers materials only when needed, eliminating large stock holdings. Key advantage: reduced warehousing cost and capital tied up in stock. Key disadvantage: total dependency on supplier reliability — a late delivery stops production immediately with no buffer stock to absorb the delay.

Material Requirements Planning (MRP)

Material requirements planning (MRP) is a computer-based approach that takes the production schedule (what products are to be made, in what quantities and by when) and works backwards through the bill of materials for each product to calculate exactly what raw materials and components must be ordered and when. MRP provides detailed ordering schedules, reduces the risk of running out of stock, and highlights when resources such as machine capacity and labour are insufficient to meet the schedule. Advantages include improved coordination between production and procurement, reduced waste from over-ordering, and better visibility of future capacity requirements. Disadvantages include the significant cost and complexity of implementing and maintaining MRP software, and the fact that MRP is only as accurate as the data fed into it — errors in the bill of materials or inaccurate lead-time data will cascade into incorrect ordering decisions.

JIT is a production philosophy — it drives the entire approach to scheduling and supplier management with the goal of eliminating inventory. MRP is a planning tool — a software system that calculates ordering schedules from a production plan. In practice many companies use MRP to plan their ordering schedules while also applying JIT principles to minimise stock levels. They are complementary rather than mutually exclusive approaches. An exam question asking you to distinguish between them should focus on: JIT = production philosophy, pull-driven, minimal stock; MRP = computer-based calculation tool, push-driven from production schedule.

Lean Manufacturing and the Seven Wastes

Lean manufacturing is a philosophy developed from the Toyota Production System that seeks to eliminate waste (called "muda" in Japanese) from every aspect of production. The central insight is that any activity consuming time, materials or labour without creating value for the customer is waste that should be eliminated or minimised. Seven categories of waste are identified in lean manufacturing, and understanding each one is essential for the OCR exam.

The seven wastes are: Transportation — unnecessary movement of materials between locations adds time and risk of damage without adding value. Inventory — holding more stock than needed ties up capital and space. Movement — unnecessary movement of people (operators walking to fetch tools, bending to reach components) wastes time and risks injury. Waiting — time spent by operators or machines idle (waiting for materials, instructions or the previous operation) adds lead time without adding value. Over-processing — carrying out more operations or finishing to a higher standard than the customer requires (for example, polishing a surface that will be hidden inside an assembly). Over-production — making more than is needed, earlier than needed — widely considered the most damaging waste because it generates all other wastes. Defects — products that do not meet specification require rework or scrapping, wasting all materials and labour invested in them.

Key Fact

The seven categories of lean waste are: Transportation, Inventory, Movement, Waiting, Over-processing, Over-production, Defects. The mnemonic TIM WOOD helps recall them. Over-production is considered the most damaging because it generates all other wastes — for example, producing too many parts creates excess inventory, which requires transportation, which risks damage (defects).

Reducing transportation waste cuts lead time and damage risk. Reducing inventory frees up capital and floor space and improves responsiveness to design changes. Reducing movement waste by redesigning workstation layouts improves operator productivity and reduces musculoskeletal injury. Reducing waiting by synchronising production stages (balanced production flow) increases throughput. Reducing over-processing by specifying only the quality level customers require cuts cycle time. Reducing over-production by only making to order (pull production) eliminates the need to hold finished goods stock. Reducing defects cuts scrap, rework and warranty costs, and improves customer satisfaction. Each waste reduction directly improves efficiency, responsiveness and cost.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about the seven wastes, always identify the waste by its correct name and then explain specifically how eliminating it improves production — don't just say 'it saves time'. For example: 'reducing waiting waste by synchronising the output rate of each work station to match the next operation eliminates idle time and increases throughput without increasing machine investment.' For JIT questions, always include a limitation — production lines stopping due to a late delivery is the classic answer. If asked to compare JIT and MRP, use the contrast: JIT is a production philosophy; MRP is a computer-based calculation tool.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Just-in-time manufacturing orders materials only when needed, cutting inventory costs but creating total dependency on supplier reliability — a late delivery stops production with no buffer.
  • Material requirements planning (MRP) is a computer-based system that calculates what to order, in what quantity and when, based on the production schedule and bill of materials — complementing JIT by providing the ordering schedule.
  • The seven lean wastes — Transportation, Inventory, Movement, Waiting, Over-processing, Over-production, Defects (TIM WOOD) — represent all activities that consume resources without adding customer value; eliminating each directly improves throughput, cost and quality.

glossary_terms.definition: The management of the ordering, storage and movement of materials and components to ensure production needs are met without holding excessive stock.
A production philosophy in which materials and components are ordered and delivered only when needed in the production process, eliminating large stock holdings.
A computer-based system that calculates what materials are needed, in what quantity and by when, based on the production schedule and bill of materials.
A systematic approach to manufacturing that focuses on eliminating all forms of waste — any activity that consumes resources without adding value for the customer.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the main disadvantage of just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing?
A) It requires very large warehouse facilities to store excess components
B) It leads to over-production and excess finished goods
C) A late supplier delivery can stop the entire production line with no buffer stock
D) It prevents manufacturers from using computer-aided production planning
practice_questions.marks: C) A late supplier delivery can stop the entire production line with no buffer stock [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two of the seven categories of lean waste.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: Transportation / Inventory / Movement / Waiting / Over-processing / Over-production / Defects. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how reducing the waste of 'waiting' can improve manufacturing performance.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that waiting is idle time when operators or machines are not productive. Second mark: by synchronising the output rate of each workstation (balancing the production flow), waiting is eliminated so every stage operates continuously. Third mark: this directly increases throughput — more units are completed per hour without any additional capital investment in machinery. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by material requirements planning (MRP) and give one advantage of using it over ordering materials manually.
practice_questions.marks: Description (2 marks): MRP is a computer-based system that takes the production schedule and, using the bill of materials for each product, calculates exactly what raw materials and components must be ordered, in what quantities, and by what date to ensure production is not delayed (2 marks for a full description; 1 mark for a basic description). Advantage (2 marks): MRP automatically highlights when materials will run short before a stockout actually occurs, allowing the purchasing team to place orders in time to avoid a production stoppage — something that would be difficult to track manually across hundreds of components (2 marks for a developed, applied advantage; 1 mark for a basic statement). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer of precision components is experiencing high levels of inventory waste and over-production. The production manager wants to introduce lean manufacturing principles.

Discuss the actions the production manager could take to reduce inventory waste and over-production, and the benefits and challenges of doing so.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering specific lean actions for each waste (e.g. introducing pull production / kanban signals for over-production so components are only made when the next stage requests them; implementing JIT ordering to reduce raw material stock for inventory waste), the benefits (reduced capital tied up, more floor space, greater responsiveness), and challenges (requires reliable suppliers for JIT; pull production requires smooth, synchronised production stages — any bottleneck creates waiting; staff need training in the new system). Both wastes addressed with development.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two relevant points developed with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One waste addressed with a basic action.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A car components manufacturer currently operates a traditional push-production system with large raw material and work-in-progress stock holdings. It is considering switching to a full just-in-time system.

Evaluate the extent to which adopting JIT would improve the company's overall manufacturing performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies JIT's genuine performance improvements (eliminated warehousing costs, capital freed from stock holdings, reduced obsolescence risk as components change, faster response to customer demand changes, forces process discipline that often uncovers other inefficiencies), then challenges these with specific risks for this company (car components depend on a complex global supply chain — a single delayed delivery stops the line; the 2021 semiconductor shortage demonstrated how JIT-style supply chains collapse under disruption; initial transition costs are high as supplier contracts and logistics are renegotiated). Reaches a clear substantiated judgement — e.g. JIT would improve cost and responsiveness in stable conditions but creates fragility in the supply chain; a hybrid approach (JIT for high-volume, reliable-supply components; small strategic buffer stocks for high-risk or single-source parts) may be optimal.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to the car components context and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which inventory management approach orders materials only when they are needed in the production process?
Which of the seven lean wastes is considered the most damaging because it generates all other wastes?
MRP calculates what materials are needed, in what quantity and by when, using the production schedule and the _____ for each product.
The mnemonic TIM WOOD stands for Transportation, Inventory, Movement, Waiting, Over-processing, Over-production and _____.
Match each lean waste to the correct description of how reducing it improves production.
right: Eliminating rework and scrap reduces material and labour costs and improves customer satisfaction
Reducing unnecessary movement of materials cuts lead time and damage risk
Synchronising production stages increases throughput without additional capital investment

flashcard_questions.a: JIT is a production philosophy where materials are ordered and delivered only when needed, eliminating large stock holdings and reducing warehousing costs.

flashcard_questions.q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of JIT manufacturing.
flashcard_questions.a: Advantage: reduced capital tied up in stock; disadvantage: a late supplier delivery stops the entire production line immediately with no buffer stock.
MRP is a computer-based system that calculates what materials to order, in what quantity and by when, using the production schedule and the bill of materials.

flashcard_questions.q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of MRP.
flashcard_questions.a: Advantage: prevents stockouts by generating advance ordering schedules; disadvantage: it is only as accurate as the data entered — errors in the bill of materials cascade through all ordering decisions.
Lean manufacturing is an approach that systematically eliminates all forms of waste — activities that consume resources without adding value for the customer.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the seven categories of lean waste using the mnemonic TIM WOOD.
flashcard_questions.a: Transportation, Inventory, Movement, Waiting, Over-processing, Over-production, Defects — each represents activities consuming resources without adding customer value.

flashcard_questions.q: What is 'over-production' waste and why is it considered the most damaging lean waste?
flashcard_questions.a: Over-production is making more than is needed or earlier than needed; it is the most damaging because it generates all other wastes such as excess inventory, transportation and storage costs.

flashcard_questions.q: What is 'waiting' waste in lean manufacturing?
flashcard_questions.a: Waiting waste is idle time when operators or machines are not productive because they are waiting for materials, instructions or the previous operation to finish.
Over-processing waste means carrying out more operations or finishing to a higher standard than the customer actually requires, consuming time and materials unnecessarily.

flashcard_questions.q: How does reducing 'defects' waste improve manufacturing performance?
flashcard_questions.a: Reducing defects eliminates rework and scrap costs, saves all the materials and labour invested in faulty parts, and directly improves customer satisfaction and returns rates.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between JIT and MRP?
flashcard_questions.a: JIT is a production philosophy aiming to eliminate inventory; MRP is a computer-based calculation tool that generates ordering schedules from the production plan — they are complementary.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does reducing inventory waste free up more than just storage space?
flashcard_questions.a: Reducing inventory frees up capital tied up in unsold stock, reduces the risk of materials becoming obsolete, and exposes process inefficiencies previously hidden by excess buffer stock.
